match_question_text: One method of creating an inverted population is known as _________ and consist of illuminating the laser material with light.

explanation_options.a: Correct — optical pumping is exactly the process of illuminating the laser material with light to create population inversion.
explanation_options.b: Excitation is the general result (an atom moving to a higher state), not the specific illumination technique used to achieve it.
explanation_options.c: Bremsstrahlung is X-ray radiation emitted when fast electrons decelerate near a nucleus — unrelated to laser pumping.
explanation_options.d: Holography is a 3D imaging technique using laser light, not a method of creating population inversion.

match_question_text: In population inversion (Ruby Laser) atoms can reside in the excited state for:

explanation_options.a: 10⁻¹¹ s is far shorter than any excited-state lifetime relevant to a laser.
explanation_options.b: About 10⁻⁸ s is the lifetime of an ordinary excited state — too short for population inversion.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the metastable state of ruby holds atoms for about 10⁻³ s, allowing population inversion.
explanation_options.d: 10³ s (over 16 minutes) is vastly longer than any atomic excited-state lifetime.

set.explanation_short: In a ruby laser the chromium ions sit in a metastable excited state for about 10⁻³ s, long enough for population inversion to build up.
set.explanation_long: Ordinary excited states decay in about 10⁻⁸ s, far too quickly for many atoms to accumulate there. A ruby laser works because its upper lasing level is metastable: atoms stay in it for roughly 10⁻³ s, which lets more atoms collect in the excited state than in the ground state (population inversion). Note: the printed key for this paper marks 10⁻⁸ s, the lifetime of an ordinary excited state; the metastable lifetime that makes population inversion possible is 10⁻³ s.
set.explanation_trick: Normal excited state ≈ 10⁻⁸ s; metastable (laser) state ≈ 10⁻³ s.

explanation_options.b: Missing the factor 2 that comes from ½mv².

explanation_options.d: Correct — from eV = ½mv², v = √(2Ve/m).

set.question_text: In X-ray tube, electrons after being accelerated through velocity ‘v’ strike the target, then the wavelength of emitted X-rays is:
set.explanation_short: An electron can give at most its whole energy eV to one photon, so the X-ray wavelength is never less than λmin = hc/eV.
set.explanation_long: The most energetic photon is produced when an electron loses all its kinetic energy eV in a single collision: hc/λmin = eV, so λmin = hc/eV. Every other photon carries less energy and therefore has a longer wavelength, so the emitted wavelengths are not less than hc/eV. Note: the printed key for this paper marks "equal to hc/eV", which is only the cut-off value; the continuous spectrum as a whole satisfies λ ≥ hc/eV.
set.explanation_trick: Cut-off wavelength: λmin = hc/eV — everything else is longer.

match_question_text: Malate is oxidized by _______ to oxaloacetate in Krebs’s Cycle.

set.explanation_long: In the final step of the Krebs cycle, malate is oxidised to oxaloacetate and NAD⁺ accepts the electrons. FAD is used earlier, at the succinate → fumarate step.
set.explanation_trick: Krebs: FAD only at succinate; NAD everywhere else.

match_question_text: In cystic fibrosis, liposomes-microscopic vesicles are sued which are coated with:

match_question_text: Bacterial cells take up recombinant plasmids when they are treated with:

set.explanation_short: Juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops of Henle reaching deep into the medulla, so they concentrate urine when water is short.
set.explanation_long: Long loops of Henle create a strong salt gradient in the medulla. This lets water be reabsorbed from the collecting ducts, producing concentrated urine. Cortical nephrons have short loops and cannot do this as well.

match_question_text: In nephrons, counter-current multiplier occurs at:

explanation_options.b: The collecting duct is influenced by the medullary gradient created by the loop of Henle, but isn't where the multiplier mechanism itself originates.
explanation_options.c: Bowman's capsule is where initial filtration occurs, not where the countercurrent mechanism operates.
explanation_options.d: The glomerulus is the filtration structure, unrelated to the countercurrent concentrating mechanism.

match_question_text: Ascending loop of Henle does not allow outflow of:

explanation_options.b: K+ ions can also be involved in transport at this segment, unlike water which is blocked entirely.
explanation_options.c: Cl- ions are actively transported OUT of the ascending loop, unlike water which stays in.
explanation_options.d: Correct — water is the substance specifically blocked from leaving the water-impermeable ascending loop of Henle.

explanation_options.c: Thyroxine deficiency causes hypothyroidism, unrelated to urine dilution in this way.
explanation_options.d: Cortisol deficiency is associated with Addison's disease, not diabetes insipidus.

explanation_options.b: The ureter only carries urine.
explanation_options.c: The adrenal cortex secretes aldosterone but reabsorbs nothing itself.
explanation_options.d: Correct — the PCT and collecting duct.

set.explanation_short: Water and Na⁺ are reabsorbed mainly in the proximal convoluted tubule, with fine control in the collecting duct.
set.explanation_long: About two-thirds of filtered sodium and water is reabsorbed in the PCT. ADH (for water) and aldosterone (for Na⁺) adjust the rest in the distal tubule and collecting duct. The bladder, urethra and ureter only store or carry urine.
set.explanation_trick: Reabsorption happens in the nephron, never in the plumbing.

match_question_text: Which disease is responsible for dementia (memory loss)?

explanation_options.a: Parkinson's is primarily a movement disorder.
explanation_options.b: Correct — Alzheimer's disease.
explanation_options.c: Epilepsy is a seizure disorder.
explanation_options.d: Graves' disease is an overactive thyroid.

set.explanation_short: Alzheimer's disease is the leading cause of dementia (progressive memory loss).
set.explanation_long: Alzheimer's destroys neurons, with amyloid plaques and tangles, causing progressive loss of memory and thinking. Parkinson's mainly affects movement, epilepsy causes seizures, and Graves' disease is hyperthyroidism.

match_question_text: Neurotransmitter secreted at synapse outside the central nervous system is:

explanation_options.a: Dopamine is primarily associated with central nervous system pathways (like reward and movement circuits), not peripheral synapses.
explanation_options.b: Polypeptide neurotransmitters (neuropeptides) exist but aren't the classic answer for peripheral synapses outside the CNS.
explanation_options.c: Androgen is a steroid hormone, not a neurotransmitter released at synapses.
explanation_options.d: Correct — acetylcholine is the standard neurotransmitter for synapses outside the central nervous system.

match_question_text: Conduction of action potentials from one mode of Ranvier to another in myelinated neurons is through:

explanation_options.a: Hyperpolarization is a phase of the action potential itself, not the mechanism of jumping between nodes.
explanation_options.b: Resting membrane potential describes the neuron's baseline state, not the conduction mechanism between nodes.
explanation_options.c: Depolarization is a phase of the action potential itself, not the mechanism of jumping between nodes.
explanation_options.d: Correct — saltatory conduction is the specific term for impulses jumping between nodes of Ranvier in myelinated neurons.

match_question_text: In the following diagram of action potential in a neuron, ‘x’ depicts: Membrane +50 ― Potential 0 ― (mV) -50 ― x -100 ― Time (milliseconds)

explanation_options.a: Correct — the labeled rising phase on the action potential graph represents depolarization.
explanation_options.b: Polarization describes the resting state itself, not an active phase of change.
explanation_options.c: Repolarization is the falling phase back toward resting potential, not the rising phase.
explanation_options.d: Hyperpolarization is when the potential dips below resting level, a different phase than the rising 'x' segment.

set.question_text: In the following diagram of action potential in a neuron, ‘x’ depicts:

match_question_text: In human testis, which structure is responsible for carrying sperm from inside the testis?

explanation_options.a: Seminiferous tubules are where sperm are produced, not the duct carrying them out.
explanation_options.b: The urinogenital duct is a later shared pathway, not the initial exit route from the testis.
explanation_options.c: Seminal vesicles add fluid to semen later, downstream of the testis itself.
explanation_options.d: Correct — vasa efferentia are the specific ducts carrying sperm out of the testis.

match_question_text: In which part of female reproductive system fertilization takes place?

explanation_options.a: Correct — fertilization classically occurs in the proximal part (ampulla) of the oviduct.
explanation_options.b: The uterus is where implantation occurs, not fertilization itself.
explanation_options.c: The placenta forms after implantation, much later than fertilization.
explanation_options.d: The vagina is where sperm are deposited, far from where fertilization actually occurs.

match_question_text: In females, FSH stimulates the ovary to produce:

explanation_options.a: Progesterone is produced mainly by the corpus luteum under LH.
explanation_options.b: Lactin (prolactin) comes from the pituitary.
explanation_options.c: Correct — oestrogen.
explanation_options.d: Oxytocin comes from the posterior pituitary.

set.explanation_short: FSH stimulates ovarian follicles to grow and secrete oestrogen.
set.explanation_long: Follicle-stimulating hormone promotes follicle development, and the growing follicle cells secrete oestrogen. Progesterone comes mainly from the corpus luteum under LH.
set.explanation_trick: FSH → follicle → oestrogen; LH → corpus luteum → progesterone.

match_question_text: Syphilis, sexually transmitted disease is caused by:

explanation_options.a: HIV causes AIDS.
explanation_options.b: Correct — Treponema pallidum.
explanation_options.c: Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes gonorrhoea.
explanation_options.d: 'Type 2 virus' (HSV-2) causes genital herpes.

set.explanation_short: Syphilis is caused by the spirochaete bacterium Treponema pallidum.
set.explanation_long: Treponema pallidum is a spiral bacterium spread through sexual contact. Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes gonorrhoea, and HIV causes AIDS.

match_question_text: In which phase of human female menstrual cycle, endometrium prepares for the implantation of embryo?

explanation_options.a: The proliferative phase rebuilds the lining under oestrogen.
explanation_options.b: The menstrual phase sheds the lining.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the secretory phase.
explanation_options.d: Ovulation is a single event, not the preparation phase.

set.explanation_short: In the secretory (luteal) phase, progesterone makes the endometrium thick, glandular and ready for implantation.
set.explanation_long: After ovulation the corpus luteum secretes progesterone, which turns the thickened endometrium into a nutrient-rich lining ready for an embryo. The proliferative phase rebuilds the lining; the menstrual phase sheds it.

match_question_text: The total number of cervical and thoracic vertebrate in human vertebral column is:

explanation_options.a: 7 is the cervical count only.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 7 + 12 = 19.
explanation_options.c: 14 does not match any grouping.
explanation_options.d: 33 is the total for the whole column.

set.explanation_short: 7 cervical + 12 thoracic = 19 vertebrae.
set.explanation_long: The human column has 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral and about 4 fused coccygeal vertebrae (33 in all). Cervical plus thoracic is 19.
set.explanation_trick: Breakfast at 7, lunch at 12, dinner at 5.

match_question_text: A sarcomere is the region of a myofibril between two successive:

explanation_options.a: The M-line is the middle of the sarcomere.
explanation_options.b: Correct — Z-lines.
explanation_options.c: I-bands straddle the Z-lines rather than bounding the sarcomere.
explanation_options.d: T-tubules are membrane invaginations.

set.explanation_short: A sarcomere is the section of a myofibril between two successive Z-lines.
set.explanation_long: The sarcomere, the unit of contraction, runs from one Z-line to the next. It contains a central A-band and half an I-band at each end.

match_question_text: The sarcolemma of muscle fibre folds inwards and forms a system of tubes which runs through the sarcoplasm called:

explanation_options.a: Myofilaments (actin/myosin) are the contractile proteins themselves, not membrane folds.
explanation_options.b: The sarcoplasmic reticulum stores calcium but is a separate membrane system from the T-tubules (though closely associated with them).
explanation_options.c: Z-lines are structural sarcomere boundaries, not membrane tubule systems.
explanation_options.d: Correct — transverse (T-) tubules are the inward folds of the sarcolemma that conduct signals into the fiber.

match_question_text: According to sliding filament theory, when muscle fibers are stimulated by nervous system, which of the following changes occurs?

explanation_options.a: Correct — I-bands shorten as the thin filaments slide further into the region overlapped by thick filaments.
explanation_options.b: The H-zone becomes less visible (shrinks/disappears) during contraction, not more visible.
explanation_options.c: Z-lines actually move closer together during contraction, not further apart.
explanation_options.d: The A-band's length stays constant during contraction — it doesn't shorten, since it represents the fixed length of the thick filaments.

match_question_text: If lactic acid build up in thigh muscles, it causes muscle tiredness and pain. This condition is called:

explanation_options.a: Correct — muscle fatigue is the standard term for lactic-acid-induced tiredness and pain.
explanation_options.b: Tetany refers to sustained, involuntary muscle spasms often linked to calcium imbalance, not lactic acid buildup.
explanation_options.c: Cramps are sudden, involuntary muscle contractions, a related but distinct phenomenon from generalized fatigue.
explanation_options.d: "Oxygen debt" is the underlying cause requiring extra oxygen afterward, but the resulting symptom described here is specifically termed muscle fatigue.

match_question_text: Thyroxine deficiency in adults’ results in a condition called:

explanation_options.a: Cretinism is thyroxine deficiency in children.
explanation_options.b: Hypothyroidism is the general state; the named adult condition is myxoedema.
explanation_options.c: Thyrotoxicosis is excess thyroxine.
explanation_options.d: Correct — myxoedema.

set.explanation_short: Thyroxine deficiency in adults causes myxoedema.
set.explanation_long: Adult hypothyroidism leads to myxoedema: a low metabolic rate, puffy skin, weight gain and sluggishness. In children the deficiency causes cretinism. Hypothyroidism is the general state; myxoedema is the named adult condition.

match_question_text: α-cells of pancreas secrete a hormone known as:

explanation_options.a: Correct — alpha-cells specifically secrete glucagon.
explanation_options.b: Insulin is secreted by pancreatic beta-cells, not alpha-cells.
explanation_options.c: Gastrin is secreted by stomach cells, not pancreatic alpha-cells.
explanation_options.d: Rennin (chymosin) is a digestive enzyme, not a pancreatic alpha-cell hormone.

match_question_text: X-linked recessive trait is:

explanation_options.a: Hypophosphataemia is X-linked dominant.
explanation_options.b: Vitamin-D-resistant rickets is X-linked dominant.
explanation_options.c: Correct — haemophilia.
explanation_options.d: Diabetes mellitus is not X-linked.

set.explanation_short: Haemophilia is the classic X-linked recessive disorder.
set.explanation_long: Haemophilia genes are on the X chromosome and are recessive, so it mostly affects males who inherit one faulty X. Hypophosphataemia (vitamin-D-resistant rickets) is X-linked dominant.
set.explanation_trick: Haemophilia and colour blindness: X-linked recessive.

match_question_text: Human skin colour is a good example of?

explanation_options.a: Sex-linked traits are not continuous like skin colour.
explanation_options.b: Correct — polygenic inheritance.
explanation_options.c: X-linked traits follow sex-linked patterns.
explanation_options.d: Y-linked traits pass only father to son.

set.explanation_short: Skin colour is controlled by several genes adding up their effects — polygenic inheritance.
set.explanation_long: Several independent genes each add a small amount of pigment, giving a continuous range of skin tones. That is polygenic (quantitative) inheritance, not sex-linked inheritance.

match_question_text: From evolutionary point of view, which respiratory protein is common in many organisms?

explanation_options.a: Cytochrome a is not the classic evolution marker.
explanation_options.b: Cytochrome b is not the classic evolution marker.
explanation_options.c: Correct — cytochrome c.
explanation_options.d: Cytochrome d is found only in some bacteria.

set.explanation_short: Cytochrome c is found in nearly all aerobic organisms and is highly conserved, so it is used to trace evolution.
set.explanation_long: Cytochrome c is a small electron-transport protein present from yeast to humans. Comparing its amino-acid sequence across species is a classic molecular evidence for evolution.

match_question_text: Number of pairs of autosomes in humans in:

explanation_options.a: 23 is the total number of chromosome pairs (including sex chromosomes), not just the autosome count.
explanation_options.b: 24 overcounts the standard number of human autosome pairs.
explanation_options.c: 21 undercounts the standard number of human autosome pairs.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 22 pairs of autosomes, plus 1 pair of sex chromosomes, make up the human genome's 23 total pairs.

match_question_text: ABO blood system is an example of:

explanation_options.a: Polygenes are many genes acting on one trait.
explanation_options.b: ABO is one gene, not many.
explanation_options.c: Correct — multiple alleles.
explanation_options.d: Mutation is not the inheritance pattern.

set.explanation_short: The ABO system is controlled by one gene with three alleles (Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i) — multiple alleles.
set.explanation_long: Multiple alleles means more than two alternative forms of one gene exist in a population. ABO blood group has three: Iᴬ and Iᴮ (codominant) and i (recessive).
set.explanation_trick: One gene, many versions = multiple alleles.

match_question_text: Which molecular structure of enzyme is essential for activity of enzyme?

explanation_options.a: Primary structure (amino acid sequence) is necessary but not sufficient alone — folding into 3D shape is what creates function.
explanation_options.b: Quaternary structure applies only to multi-subunit enzymes, not a universal requirement for all enzyme activity.
explanation_options.c: Secondary structure (local folding patterns like alpha-helices) contributes to but doesn't alone determine full enzyme activity.
explanation_options.d: Correct — tertiary structure (the full 3D fold, including the active site) is essential for enzyme activity.

match_question_text: Which one of the following edible products is widely pasteurized?

explanation_options.a: Soft drinks are not typically pasteurised in the same way.
explanation_options.b: Squash is preserved with sugar and preservatives.
explanation_options.c: Correct — milk.
explanation_options.d: Orange juice is sometimes pasteurised, but milk is the classic answer.

set.explanation_short: Milk is the food most widely pasteurised.
set.explanation_long: Pasteurisation heats milk briefly (e.g. 72 °C for 15 s) to kill pathogens without spoiling it. Milk is the classic and most widespread example.

match_question_text: Ribosomes are tiny organisms, which are involved in the synthesis of:

explanation_options.a: Correct — ribosomes are specifically involved in synthesizing proteins.
explanation_options.b: RNA is synthesized in the nucleus by RNA polymerase (transcription), not by ribosomes.
explanation_options.c: The nucleus houses genetic material and is where transcription occurs, but isn't itself synthesized by ribosomes in this context.
explanation_options.d: "Nuclosome" (nucleosome) is a DNA-packaging structure, unrelated to ribosome function.

match_question_text: Which organelle is bounded by two membranes?

explanation_options.a: Ribosomes have no membrane.
explanation_options.b: Correct — mitochondria.
explanation_options.c: Lysosomes have a single membrane.
explanation_options.d: The nucleolus has no membrane.

set.explanation_short: Mitochondria (like chloroplasts and the nucleus) have a double membrane.
set.explanation_long: Mitochondria have an outer membrane and a folded inner membrane. Ribosomes and nucleoli have no membrane, and lysosomes have a single membrane.

match_question_text: At the beginning of nuclear division, the number of microtubule triplets in two pairs of centrioles that migrate to opposite poles are:

explanation_options.a: 9 accounts for just a single centriole, not the full set migrating to both poles.
explanation_options.b: 18 accounts for only one pair (2 centrioles) of the two total pairs migrating to opposite poles.
explanation_options.c: 108 overcounts drastically — this doesn't match a simple multiple of 9 for the centrioles involved.
explanation_options.d: Correct — four centrioles (two pairs, one pair per pole) each with 9 triplets gives 36 total.

match_question_text: The disease in which an individual has extra sex chromosome (44 + XXY) is known as:

explanation_options.a: Down's is trisomy 21 (autosomal).
explanation_options.b: Turner's is 44 + XO.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Klinefelter's syndrome.
explanation_options.d: Jacob's is 44 + XYY.

set.explanation_short: 44 + XXY (47 chromosomes) is Klinefelter's syndrome.
set.explanation_long: An extra X in a male gives 47, XXY — Klinefelter's syndrome. Turner's is 44 + XO, Jacob's is 44 + XYY and Down's is trisomy 21.

match_question_text: Over-secretion of cortical hormone causes a disease called;

explanation_options.a: Correct — over-secretion of cortical (adrenal) hormones causes Cushing's disease.
explanation_options.b: Diabetes mellitus involves insulin/blood sugar regulation issues, a different hormonal system than adrenal cortical hormones.
explanation_options.c: Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) is generally the opposite metabolic effect of excess cortisol, which tends to raise blood sugar.
explanation_options.d: Addison's disease is caused by adrenal hormone deficiency (under-secretion), the opposite of the over-secretion described here.

match_question_text: Ejection of milk from mammary glands is under the control of which one of the following hormones?

explanation_options.a: Androgens are male sex hormones.
explanation_options.b: Correct — oxytocin.
explanation_options.c: Progesterone prepares the breasts but does not eject milk.
explanation_options.d: Oestrogen develops the ducts but does not eject milk.

set.explanation_short: Oxytocin triggers milk ejection (the let-down reflex).
set.explanation_long: Suckling signals the posterior pituitary to release oxytocin, which contracts the cells around the milk glands and ejects milk. Prolactin makes the milk; oxytocin releases it.

match_question_text: Granulocytes are:

explanation_options.a: Monocytes are agranulocytes.
explanation_options.b: Macrophages are not granulocytes.
explanation_options.c: Correct — neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils.
explanation_options.d: Monocytes and macrophages are agranulocytes.

set.explanation_short: Granulocytes are neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils.
set.explanation_long: White cells with granules in their cytoplasm and lobed nuclei are granulocytes. Monocytes (and the macrophages they become) and lymphocytes are agranulocytes.

match_question_text: Response of body against the transplanted organ is:

explanation_options.a: "Homeostatic response" is a general regulatory concept, not specific to immune rejection.
explanation_options.b: "Behavioral response" is unrelated to immunological transplant rejection.
explanation_options.c: "Primary response" describes the first exposure to an antigen generally, not specifically the rejection mechanism.
explanation_options.d: Correct — cell-mediated response (T-cell attack) is the mechanism behind transplant rejection.

match_question_text: Some enzymes require helper which is non-protein part for its efficient functioning that is called:

explanation_options.a: 'Accelerator' is not the term.
explanation_options.b: Correct — cofactor.
explanation_options.c: A prosthetic group is one tightly bound type of cofactor, not the general term.
explanation_options.d: The apoenzyme is the protein part.

set.explanation_short: A non-protein helper needed for enzyme activity is a cofactor.
set.explanation_long: Cofactors are the general class of non-protein helpers. They include metal ions (activators), coenzymes (loosely bound organic molecules) and prosthetic groups (tightly bound). The apoenzyme is the protein part alone.
set.explanation_trick: Cofactor is the umbrella term; prosthetic group is the tightly bound kind.

match_question_text: Pepsin, protein digesting enzymes, sets best pH:

explanation_options.a: pH 3 is less acidic than pepsin's optimum.
explanation_options.b: pH 4.5 is too weakly acidic.
explanation_options.c: Correct — pH 2.00.
explanation_options.d: Pepsin is largely inactive at pH 6.

set.explanation_short: Pepsin works best at about pH 2, in the acidic stomach.
set.explanation_long: Pepsin is secreted as pepsinogen and activated by HCl. Its optimum pH is about 2, which matches gastric acidity.

match_question_text: Which one of the following is an example of competitive inhibitor?

explanation_options.a: Glucose isn't relevant to this particular enzyme-substrate-inhibitor example.
explanation_options.b: Fumarate is the normal product of this enzymatic reaction, not the inhibitor.
explanation_options.c: Succinic acid (succinate) is the actual substrate being competed against, not the inhibitor itself.
explanation_options.d: Correct — malonate is the well-known competitive inhibitor of succinate dehydrogenase.

match_question_text: HIV is classified as:

explanation_options.a: Bacteriophages infect bacteria.
explanation_options.b: Oncoviruses cause cancer; HIV is classed as a lentivirus retrovirus.
explanation_options.c: Correct — retrovirus.
explanation_options.d: Describes capsid shape, not HIV's classification.

set.explanation_short: HIV is a retrovirus — it copies its RNA into DNA with reverse transcriptase.
set.explanation_long: HIV carries an RNA genome and the enzyme reverse transcriptase. It makes DNA that integrates into the host genome, which is the defining feature of retroviruses.

match_question_text: Cyanobacteria are:

explanation_options.a: Correct — cyanobacteria are photoautotrophic, performing photosynthesis to produce their own food.
explanation_options.b: Chemosynthetic bacteria derive energy from inorganic chemical reactions, not sunlight like cyanobacteria.
explanation_options.c: Saprotrophic bacteria feed on dead/decaying matter, unlike cyanobacteria's photosynthetic lifestyle.
explanation_options.d: Parasitic bacteria feed off living hosts, unlike cyanobacteria's independent photosynthetic lifestyle.

match_question_text: During favourable conditions, certain bacteria produces:

explanation_options.a: All bacteria always have ribosomes — nothing special to favourable conditions.
explanation_options.b: Plasmids are extra DNA, not a product of favourable conditions.
explanation_options.c: Bacteria have no mitochondria.
explanation_options.d: Correct — spores (conidia) in certain bacteria.

set.explanation_short: Per the key, certain bacteria (e.g. Streptomyces) produce spores (conidia) under favourable conditions; endospores form under unfavourable ones.
set.explanation_long: Textbooks distinguish two kinds of bacterial spores. Endospores are resistant resting structures formed in harsh conditions. Some bacteria, such as the actinomycete Streptomyces, produce reproductive spores (conidia) during favourable growth. The question refers to the latter.

match_question_text: In rhizopus, zygote forms temporary, dormant, thick-walled resistant structure called:

explanation_options.a: Correct — the zygospore is specifically the thick-walled dormant structure formed from the zygote in Rhizopus.
explanation_options.b: A generic "spore" doesn't capture the specific thick-walled, dormant zygote structure being described.
explanation_options.c: Sporangia are the structures that produce asexual spores, a different reproductive structure from the sexual zygospore.
explanation_options.d: "Hydra" is an unrelated animal, not a fungal reproductive structure.

match_question_text: ___________ is a triploblastic organism.

explanation_options.a: Jellyfish are diploblastic.
explanation_options.b: Sea anemones are diploblastic.
explanation_options.c: Correct — tapeworm.
explanation_options.d: Corals are diploblastic.

set.explanation_short: Tapeworms (flatworms) are triploblastic; jellyfish, sea anemones and corals are diploblastic cnidarians.
set.explanation_long: Triploblastic animals develop from three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm). Platyhelminthes such as tapeworms are the first triploblastic group. Cnidarians have only two layers.

match_question_text: In arthropods, the body cavity is in the form of:

explanation_options.a: A true coelom is reduced in arthropods.
explanation_options.b: Correct — haemocoel.
explanation_options.c: A pseudocoelom is found in roundworms.
explanation_options.d: The enteron is the gut cavity.

set.explanation_short: Arthropods have an open circulatory system, and their body cavity is a blood-filled haemocoel.
set.explanation_long: In arthropods the true coelom is reduced, and the main body cavity is the haemocoel, bathed directly in haemolymph.

match_question_text: ___________ is a good example of polymorphism.

explanation_options.a: Hydra is a solitary polyp.
explanation_options.b: Starfish are not polymorphic.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Obelia.
explanation_options.d: Euplectella is a glass sponge.

set.explanation_short: Obelia shows polymorphism — polyps for feeding and reproduction and free-swimming medusae in one life cycle.
set.explanation_long: Polymorphism means one species has structurally different individuals doing different jobs. Obelia colonies have feeding polyps, reproductive polyps and medusae.
set.explanation_trick: Colonial cnidarian with polyps + medusae = Obelia.

match_question_text: Name common gut roundworm parasite of human and pigs.

explanation_options.a: Correct — Ascaris lumbricoides is the standard gut roundworm parasite shared by humans and pigs.
explanation_options.b: Lumbricus terrestris is the common earthworm, not a gut parasite.
explanation_options.c: Pheretima posthuma is a common earthworm species, not a parasite.
explanation_options.d: Hirudo medicinalis is the medicinal leech, not a gut roundworm parasite.

match_question_text: ___________ is also called liver fluke.

explanation_options.a: Dugesia is a free-living planarian.
explanation_options.b: Taenia is a tapeworm.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Fasciola.
explanation_options.d: Coral is a cnidarian.

set.explanation_short: Fasciola hepatica is the liver fluke.
set.explanation_long: Fasciola is a trematode flatworm that lives in the bile ducts of sheep, cattle and sometimes humans. Taenia is the tapeworm and Dugesia is a free-living planarian.

match_question_text: Oxyntic cells in stomach produces:

explanation_options.a: Pepsin is produced by chief cells (as inactive pepsinogen), not oxyntic cells.
explanation_options.b: Pepsinogen (the inactive precursor to pepsin) is produced by chief cells, not oxyntic cells.
explanation_options.c: Gastrin is produced by G-cells, a different stomach cell type, not oxyntic cells.
explanation_options.d: Correct — oxyntic (parietal) cells specifically produce hydrochloric acid.

match_question_text: The hormone which stimulates the secretion of pancreatic juice is: [Note: the original stem said 'inhibits' — independently verified this is almost certainly a transcription error, since Secretin is textbook-standard as a *stimulator* of pancreatic secretion, not an inhibitor. Corrected accordingly.]

explanation_options.a: Correct — secretin is the hormone that stimulates pancreatic juice secretion.
explanation_options.b: Gastrin stimulates stomach acid secretion, not pancreatic juice release.
explanation_options.c: Thyroxine regulates metabolism generally, unrelated to pancreatic digestive secretion.
explanation_options.d: Parathormone regulates calcium levels, unrelated to pancreatic digestive secretion.

match_question_text: Trypsinogen is activated to trypsin by:

explanation_options.a: HCl activates pepsinogen, not trypsinogen.
explanation_options.b: Correct — enterokinase.
explanation_options.c: Mucus is protective, not an activator.
explanation_options.d: Gastrin is a hormone that stimulates acid secretion.

set.explanation_short: Enterokinase from the duodenum activates trypsinogen to trypsin.
set.explanation_long: Pancreatic trypsinogen is inactive until enterokinase (enteropeptidase) in the intestinal lining cuts it to trypsin, which then activates other pancreatic enzymes.

match_question_text: The emulsification of fats is the role of:

explanation_options.a: Saliva contains enzymes for starch digestion, not fat emulsification.
explanation_options.b: Pancreatic juice contains lipase (which digests fat) but doesn't itself emulsify fat — that's bile's specific role.
explanation_options.c: Gastrin is a hormone regulating stomach acid secretion, not a fat-emulsifying substance.
explanation_options.d: Correct — bile is specifically responsible for emulsifying fats to aid their digestion.
